summary: This experimental document specifies a mechanism for an RPL router to measure the aggregated values of given routing metrics along an existing route to another RPL router. This lets the router decide whether to discover a better route.

eli5.summary: A tiny network device measures how good a path is, and then decides whether to look for a better one.

questions: measure rpl routing metrics along a route
how to find better routes in low-power networks
subtitle: Measuring route quality along a path in low-power networks.

tldr.problem: In low-power lossy networks (LLNs), the RPL routing protocol builds trees optimized for reaching a root, but point-to-point routes between arbitrary nodes may be suboptimal. A router needs to measure the actual quality of an existing route before deciding whether to invest CPU and energy discovering a better one.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines Measurement Objects (MOs) that traverse a route hop-by-hop, accumulating the values of routing metrics (such as expected transmission count or link quality). When the object reaches the destination, the router sends a reply back with the measured values.
tldr.outcome: Routers can now measure route quality without consuming excessive resources. This feeds into point-to-point route discovery (P2P-RPL), helping routers set realistic constraints when searching for better routes.

today: RFC 6998 remains Experimental. It depends on the deployment of P2P-RPL (RFC 6997), which is also Experimental. The specification provides a tool for point-to-point metric measurement in low-power networks but has seen limited deployment as the broader P2P-RPL capability has not become mainstream in IoT standards.

sections.title: The Problem of Point-to-Point Routing
sections.content:
The IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-power and Lossy Networks (RPL) optimizes routes to a central root using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). However, many IoT applications need efficient point-to-point (P2P) communication between arbitrary devices. RPL's P2P routes are constrained to DAG links, which may be suboptimal, and route discovery is proactive (planned ahead), not reactive (on-demand).

The RFC 6997 extension provides reactive P2P route discovery via P2P-RPL, but a router first needs to know whether a better route is worth finding. If it already has a route of moderate quality, searching for a slightly better one wastes battery and bandwidth. This RFC provides a lightweight way to measure the quality of an existing route so the router can decide whether to search for a better one.
sections.eli5: In a small network, every device talks to a central hub, but sometimes two devices need to talk directly. Before searching for a direct path, a device should check if the existing path is really bad.

sections.title: How Measurement Objects Work
sections.content:
A Measurement Object (MO) is a special RPL control message that measures routing metrics along a route. The starting device (Start Point) creates an MO, optionally specifying metrics to measure (such as link quality, ETX, or latency). The MO travels along the route toward the destination (End Point), and each intermediate device updates the metric values. The MO accumulates the total metrics as it progresses.

When the MO reaches the End Point, it either continues to the final destination or is converted into a Measurement Reply that returns to the Start Point with all accumulated metric values. The Start Point receives the reply and learns the total cost of the route—for example, an ETX (expected transmission count) of 5.2, meaning on average 5.2 transmissions per hop are needed due to losses and retransmissions.

Two variants exist: a base MO for standard measurement, and a Secure MO that includes cryptographic protection against tampering.
sections.eli5: A message travels along the path, each stop writes down the quality of the link, and at the end all measurements are sent back to the start.

sections.title: The Measurement Object Format
sections.content:
An MO message includes several key fields. The RPLInstanceID identifies which routing instance (and DAG) is being measured. Flags control the behavior: the Type (T) flag distinguishes a Measurement Request from a Reply; the Hop-by-Hop (H) flag indicates whether the route is hop-by-hop (DAG-based) or source-routed (explicitly specified); the Accumulate Route (A) flag tells intermediate points to build a return route for the reply; the Intermediate Reply (I) flag allows an intermediate node to answer if it knows the rest of the path.

The message also carries the Start Point and End Point addresses, plus an optional Address vector that either accumulates the route as the message travels or carries a pre-specified source route. Each message includes one or more Metric Container options that hold the routing metrics being accumulated. The metrics follow the standard RPL Metric Container format defined in RFC 6550.
sections.eli5: The message is like a postcard with boxes for measurements. Each hop fills in its measurements, and the postcard passes to the next hop.

sections.title: Creating and Processing Measurement Requests
sections.content:
The Start Point initiates a Measurement Request by setting the T flag to 1 (indicating a request), choosing which metrics to measure, and setting various other flags based on the route type. If measuring a hop-by-hop route via a DAG (identified by RPLInstanceID), the Start Point uses the RPLInstanceID and End Point address to specify the route. If measuring a source route, it includes the full path in the Address vector.

As the MO travels hop-by-hop, each intermediate device determines whether it is still on the path (by checking the RPLInstanceID and routing information) and, if so, updates the metric values. When the MO reaches the End Point, it generates a Measurement Reply (with T flag set to 0) and sends it back. Optionally, an intermediate device with the I flag set may answer on the End Point's behalf if it already knows the remaining path cost.

The Start Point must maintain state for each outstanding Measurement Request (identified by the RPLInstanceID, sequence number, and End Point address) and discard replies that arrive after a timeout, since the measurement may no longer be valid.
sections.eli5: The first device writes what metrics to measure and where to send the message. Each hop updates the metrics. The last hop sends a reply back with all the totals.

sections.title: Accumulating Return Routes
sections.content:
When measuring a hop-by-hop route with a local RPLInstanceID, the Start Point can set the Accumulate Route (A) flag to request that each intermediate device add its IPv6 address to an Address vector in the message. This builds a source route that the End Point can use, after reversal, to send the Measurement Reply back along the same path.

This is useful in asymmetric networks where the return path differs from the forward path, or where the End Point might not otherwise know how to reach the Start Point efficiently. Each intermediate device appends its global or unique-local IPv6 address at the Index specified, allowing the End Point to construct a complete reverse source route.

Alternatively, if the Start Point provides a source route directly in the Address vector, intermediate devices must not modify it, ensuring the MO travels exactly the specified path.
sections.eli5: The Start Point can ask each device along the way to add its address to a list, creating a return route for the reply to come back the same way.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC defines Secure MO messages that use the RPL security framework (certificates and digital signatures) to prevent unauthorized routers from measuring routes or tampering with metrics. The Start Point determines whether to use secure measurement and selects a security configuration that is applied to both the Measurement Request and Reply.

Deployments should configure access control to prevent unauthorized routers from initiating measurements, since a measurement consumes CPU and bandwidth on multiple routers. An LLN MUST support secure MOs to prevent misuse. Implementations may also discard measurement requests from certain sources or limit the measurement rate based on policy.
sections.eli5: Only authorized devices can ask for measurements, and signatures prevent anyone from lying about the metrics.
